analysis.one_liner: Lets workers fight and sue over denied employer health insurance claims, with faster reviews and real damages.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved the bill in October 1992, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would fix the rules for people whose employer health plan denies a claim. It sets deadlines for insurers to decide claims, requires quick handling of urgent and expensive treatments, and creates a Labor Department office that helps patients appeal denials. It also lets patients recover money damages when a plan wrongly withholds benefits, forces plans to pay attorney fees when a patient wins, and opens the door for state lawsuits against insurers that handle claims unfairly. Today, a federal law called ERISA largely blocks those suits and limits recoveries.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and families covered by employer health plans, especially those whose claims for treatment are denied or delayed. Patients facing urgent care would get faster answers, and anyone wrongly denied benefits could recover actual damages plus attorney fees. A new Labor Department claims-assistance program and an arbitration/mediation system would give patients free-standing help instead of fighting a plan alone.

how_it_helps.text: Sets time limits for deciding claims and requires expedited review and automatic continued coverage for urgent, life-threatening treatments and high-value services.
Creates a Labor Department welfare benefit claims assistance program that reviews denials, helps with appeals, and contacts plans on patients' behalf.
Lets participants and beneficiaries recover actual damages from plan fiduciaries and insurance contractors who fail to provide benefits, with punitive damages where the failure is fraud.
Requires plans to pay reasonable attorney fees to patients who prevail, making it practical for ordinary people to challenge denials.
Repeals part of ERISA's preemption so state laws against unfair insurance claims practices can be enforced against insurers.
Establishes an Early Resolution Program with trained, randomly assigned arbitrators and facilitators, plus attorney referral panels including pro bono lawyers.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer-sponsored benefit plans. Insurers would face state court suits over unfair claims practices and lose the shield that currently caps their exposure; plan fiduciaries and their insurance contractors would be jointly liable for actual damages, and plans would absorb the cost of faster claims processing, disclosure of fee schedules and insurance contracts, and patient attorney fees when patients win.

drawbacks.text: The bill adds new compliance deadlines, disclosure duties, and a federal arbitration and mediation apparatus, which plan administrators and insurers said would raise the cost of running employer health plans.
Restoring state-law remedies creates a patchwork of different rules across states for the same employer plan, which employers argued raises premiums and administrative costs.

The arbitration and mediation system requires plans to participate while claimants choose the procedure, and critics of such systems note that repeat-player plans have structural advantages in repeated proceedings before a fixed roster of arbitrators.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the upside is concrete: faster answers on urgent care, a government office to help with appeals, real damages, and paid attorney fees when they win. The main cost falls on insurers and employers, who would face more litigation and administrative expense, some of which could show up in premiums. The bill was heavily amended in committee, and its arbitration system is complex, but its core purpose — ending ERISA's near-total shield for plans that wrongly deny health claims — addresses a well-documented gap in patient protection.

outcome.mechanism: The committee passed it and placed it on the House calendar in October 1992, but the House leadership never brought it up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 22, 1991 by Rep. Howard Berman with four original cosponsors and was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
It received a subcommittee hearing in July 1991 and was forwarded to the full committee in September 1991.
The full committee marked it up in July 1992, ordered it reported amended on July 30, 1992, and reported it to the House on October 5, 1992.
It was placed on the Union Calendar on October 5, 1992, where it remained without a floor vote until the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors kept the ERISA preemption shield that limits their liability for denied health claims, and patients remained unable to recover damages or sue insurers in state court over unfair claims practices.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 23 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Democratic-controlled committee reported the bill; no Republicans appear among its recorded supporters.

industries.note: ERISA preemption currently shields insurers administering employer plans from state unfair-claims-practices lawsuits and from damages awards; the bill removes that shield and makes insurers liable for actual damages when claims are wrongly denied. Their loss is the patient's remedy.

industries.industry: Employer-sponsored benefit plans and plan fiduciaries
industries.note: Plans would face strict claim-review deadlines, mandatory disclosure of insurance contracts and provider fee schedules, joint liability for actual damages, and payment of patients' attorney fees when patients prevail.

The bill creates a new category of 'insurance contractor' that is jointly and severally liable with plan fiduciaries for wrongful denial of benefits and subject to the new Early Resolution Program procedures.

industries.industry: Employment and benefits lawyers and arbitration professionals
industries.note: The Early Resolution Program's rosters of arbitrators and facilitators, attorney referral panels, and the mandatory attorney-fee provision would expand paid and pro bono legal work representing patients challenging denials.
